title: Astronomers argue Van Gogh’s Starry Night shows a real dawn sky, from about 22 July 1889
body: On 22 October 2026 a team led by astronomer Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim of Kyung Hee University in South Korea [argued in Scientific Reports](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-73025-5) that the sky in Vincent van Gogh’s The Starry Night is a real one. The clock is the Moon: from one dawn to the next it moves about 13° and changes shape, so a thin crescent standing above Venus, as in the painting, fits only a few days. The picture is usually dated to June 1889, when Van Gogh lived at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, but at dawn on 19 June the Moon was about 63% lit. Within a narrow view recovered from his sketch of the hills, the team found only three dawns in June and July 1889 with the Moon above Venus, and on 22 July the star cluster called the Hyades sat in the middle. The Van Gogh Museum, which was not involved, [told the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2026/oct/22/astronomy-dating-art-van-gogh-starry-night-painting) that he painted it in June and had a severe breakdown about 22 July; astronomer Donald Olson doubts the match, and the authors think several nights may be blended.

slides.question: At dawn on 19 June 1889, a date proposed for Van Gogh’s The Starry Night, what share of the Moon was lit?
slides.explanation: About 63%, past half: a fat Moon, not the thin crescent Van Gogh painted. The 2026 paper in Scientific Reports gives 63.1% at 2:27 a.m. at Saint-Rémy.

slides.alt: Animation in night blues: a schematic sketch after The Starry Night, then a chart of the eastern dawn sky over Saint-Rémy in 1889 with Venus and the Moon computed day by day, a narrow frame from Van Gogh's sketch, and three dawns that fit: 23 June, 22 and 23 July.
slides.music: “Canon in D for Two Harps” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Step through the dawns of June and July 1889. Find one where the Moon stands above Venus inside the narrow frame, as in the painting.
slides.takeaway: Only 23 June, 22 July and 23 July fit. The 2026 paper prefers 22 July: the Hyades sit in the middle of the frame then. On 19 June the Moon was far off, and 63% lit.

slides.alt: The Starry Night: a swirling blue night sky with a yellow crescent Moon at top right, bright stars, a dark cypress at left and a village with a church spire below hills.
slides.caption: The Starry Night (1889). The crescent Moon is at top right; the 2026 paper reads the big white star left of centre as Venus and a group of stars near the middle as the Hyades.
slides.credit: Vincent van Gogh · Museum of Modern Art, New York · Public domain

slides.heading: How a painted sky can be dated
slides.text: Star patterns hardly change in a lifetime, but the Moon and planets move. The Moon goes about 13° a day against the stars and through all its shapes in 29.5 days, so its phase and its place beside Venus work as a calendar. The paper first tested the method on other night paintings, two of them by Van Gogh.

left.label: Van Gogh Museum
left.text: In June 1889, on canvas he received in early June. A drawing after it went to his brother Theo on 2 July, and a breakdown about 22 July stopped his painting.

right.label: The 2026 paper
right.text: The sky fits the dawn of about 22 July 1889. The authors read his letters as putting the breakdown in late July, and think several nights may be blended.

slides.question: Why can the Moon help date the sky in The Starry Night when the stars alone can’t?
options: Its shape and place change daily
Stars fade within a few years
Its colour changes with the season
slides.explanation: Star patterns barely change in a lifetime, but the Moon moves about 13° a day and changes shape over 29.5 days, so a thin crescent above Venus fits only a few dawns.
